summary: When you build one game for two platforms, share the mechanics, animations and balance, give each version modes that use its own hardware strengths, and treat a stable frame rate as non-negotiable, cutting content until you hit it.
takeaways: Give each platform version a mode built on its strengths
Share mechanics, animations and balance so two versions aren't double work
Cut content until a stable 60 FPS holds
Variable character strength powers party modes, customization and amiibo
Hand parameter entry to planners; the director supervises
games: Super Smash Bros. for 3DS / Wii U

principles.principle: Give each platform version a mode built on its unique hardware strength
principles.why: A handheld means one player per screen while a home console gathers many. Linking their merits, and sharing mechanics, animations and balance, made two versions possible without double the work.
principles.how: List each platform's distinctive quality and build an exclusive mode around it, e.g., free exploration of a huge map when every player has their own screen.
principles.anti_pattern: Shipping two versions that differ only in raw graphical power.
principles.example: Smash Run on 3DS (five minutes of power-up collecting on a huge map, from Kirby Air Ride's City Trial) vs. 8-Player Smash and Smash Tour on Wii U.

principles.principle: Treat a stable 60 FPS as a must; pare content until it holds
principles.why: Many 3DS games ran at 30 FPS or dropped stereoscopic 3D. Sakurai considered 60 FPS essential, so content was cut back until four-player matches with 3D ran smoothly.
principles.how: Set the frame-rate target at the start, and when the weaker platform can't hold it, cut or simplify features (e.g., a two-character fighter) instead of lowering the target.
principles.anti_pattern: Dropping to 30 FPS or removing a headline feature like 3D to fit everything in.
principles.example: Smash for 3DS ran four players, stereoscopic 3D, items, Pokémon and Assist Trophies at 60 FPS. Ice Climbers, controlling two at once, was too much for the 3DS.
principles.quote: I considered 60 FPS gameplay to be an absolute must, so we pared things down until that was realized.

principles.principle: Use variable character strength for party modes, not level-playing-field matches
principles.why: A framework that changes character parameters enabled Smash Run, Smash Tour, custom moves, Mii Fighters and trainable amiibo, but it isn't suited to hardcore matches that need a level playing field.
principles.how: Build a parameter layer (equipment, attack/speed boosts, three variants per special move) and enable it only in casual or party modes.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting stat-altering systems leak into serious competitive play.
principles.example: amiibo CPU fighters that earn battle experience as they fight. Character Creation with three options for each special move.

principles.principle: Move parameter entry off the director onto a small planner team
principles.why: Sakurai had entered every parameter himself on earlier games despite heavy supervision, approval and marketing duties, which he says he should never have done. An efficient pipeline let planners take over.
principles.how: Build tools and pipelines that let a few planners enter and tune data, add more play testers to judge versus balance, and keep the director supervising.
principles.anti_pattern: The director personally inputting all parameters on top of every other duty.
principles.example: From Smash for 3DS / Wii U, planners handled tuning. On Ultimate, Sakurai only supervised.

summary: Full bug coverage is combinatorially impossible, so point your testing at the systems most likely to break (one character controlling another, scene changes, extreme terrain, growth and parameter systems), and re-test widely after every fix, because fixes create new bugs.
takeaways: Modern games' combinations make exhaustive bug testing impossible
Target grabs, scene changes, extreme terrain and growth systems first
Every fix can create new bugs; re-test before patching
Expecting bug-free games would make releasing games practically impossible

principles.principle: Target bug testing at likely contradiction points instead of brute-forcing combinations
principles.why: With 89 fighters there are about 8,000 pairings before moves, items, players, stages and spirits are multiplied in, so testing everything is impossible. Bugs cluster where systems fight over control.
principles.how: Test first where one entity forcibly controls another (grabs and throws, especially on a target mid special move), scene-changing super moves, extreme or V-shaped terrain, and modifier systems.
principles.anti_pattern: Brute-force testing every combination with no prioritization.
principles.example: Smash Ultimate: grabbing a fighter in the middle of a special move, Final Smashes with scene changes, Stage Builder V-shaped terrain, Spirits.

principles.principle: Re-run broad checks after every bug fix before releasing the patch
principles.why: Fixing one bug can introduce others ("enbugging"), so a fix can't simply ship right away.
principles.how: Pair each fix with a regression pass over related systems and only then release the patch.
principles.anti_pattern: Pushing a hotfix out immediately without re-checking.
principles.quote: That's because fixing one bug might introduce others. This is sometimes called "enbugging."

principles.principle: Budget test hours in proportion to parameter and growth systems
principles.why: Any game with parameters, character growth or unlockable skills is grueling to test, and a game that takes dozens of hours to finish may need thousands to tens of thousands of hours of testing.
principles.how: When adding a stat, growth or unlock system, estimate the extra test matrix it creates and reserve QA time for it in the schedule.
principles.anti_pattern: Adding modifier systems late without accounting for their testing cost.
principles.example: Smash Ultimate's Spirits system made testing a gargantuan task.

summary: Keep your ideas and specs in a collapsible hierarchical outline (heading, subheading, detail) so they stay clean and easy to reorganize, and tidy the outline before anyone else sees it.
takeaways: Organize specs and ideas in collapsible tiers
Word's View → Outline gives you this for free
Clean up personal outlines before sharing them

principles.principle: Write specs as a collapsible hierarchy: item, sub-item, then details
principles.why: A folder-like outline keeps specs clean and simple, lets you reorganize items freely, and Sakurai calls it practically indispensable for keeping track of ideas.
principles.how: Use an outline view (Word: View → Outline) with, for example, fighter name → special moves → each move's spec, collapsing the sections you aren't working on.
principles.anti_pattern: Long flat documents that are hard to navigate or reorder.
principles.example: A demo outline structured like Smash Ultimate's main menu. Fighter special-move specs.
principles.quote: It's an essential tool for organizing information, and practically indispensable for keeping track of ideas— so I really can't do without it.

principles.principle: Clean up personal idea outlines before putting them on shared servers
principles.why: Sakurai mostly uses outlines to compile his own ideas, and design documents usually end up on a shared company server, so others will read them.
principles.how: Do a cleanup pass on your private outline before sharing it as a design document.
principles.anti_pattern: Posting a raw personal idea dump as the team's spec.

summary: When characters from different art styles share one screen, pull every one of them toward a common middle (color, texture detail, proportions, design detail and real-world believability) so no one looks like they came from a different medium.
takeaways: Official designs copied as-is give an incohesive style
Mute bright primaries and let them react to light
Add detail to cartoony characters, ease textures on realistic ones
Tweak proportions and refine every design equally
Ask how features would work if characters really existed

principles.principle: Unify mixed art styles by meeting in the middle on detail
principles.why: Matching each official design would give an incohesive look. Cartoony characters have flat fills while realistic ones have rich textures, so both need adjusting toward each other.
principles.how: Add material texture to flat-shaded characters, tone down texture on realistic ones, tweak proportions slightly, and give every character the same refinement pass.
principles.anti_pattern: Importing every character's original design unchanged.
principles.example: Mario's denim textures in Brawl. Bayonetta's adjusted proportions. Olimar's suit, R.O.B.'s added detail, Ice Climbers' spiked boots.
principles.quote: Don't make it look like a fight between live action and animation.

principles.principle: Mute bright primary colors and let them respond to lighting
principles.why: In games a bright red looks roughly the same under any lighting, which clashes with characters using subdued palettes.
principles.how: Render bold reds, blues and yellows slightly paler and make them more strongly affected by light sources.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving saturated primaries flat and unlit beside realistically shaded characters.
principles.example: Smash Bros. characters originally featuring big, bold colors.

principles.principle: Ground stylized features in how they'd work if characters were real
principles.why: Thinking about how characters would look and behave if they really existed helps flesh out details so they sit naturally beside realistic characters.
principles.how: Replace comic shorthand with physical logic, e.g., have eyelids close instead of pupils shutting, and get the license holder's permission.
principles.anti_pattern: Keeping comic-book shorthand that breaks next to realistic characters.
principles.example: Donkey Kong and Yoshi's eyelids close in Smash. Donkey Kong's teeth fit together differently.

summary: Know and respect the guidelines your game must meet, since they often exist to give players consistent rules, but expect them to clash with your intent at times, and if you write guidelines yourself, leave room for leniency.
takeaways: Products that break guidelines can't be released
Consistent rules across a series make games easier to play
Guidelines may block your intent; players won't know why
Good guidelines allow a little leniency

principles.principle: Keep a series' core rules and controls consistent across releases
principles.why: Old Tetris games had no unified control scheme or rotation rules, so every version felt different, and changing the rules with every game makes it harder to play.
principles.how: Standardize the fundamentals (piece colors and shapes, rotation points, preview count, ghost-piece display, lock behavior) and keep them identical across versions.
principles.anti_pattern: Reinventing basic controls and rules in every new installment.
principles.example: The Tetris Company's 2002 guidelines, which addressed infinite rotation delaying lockdown.
principles.quote: But to be frank, changing the rules with every new game makes it harder to play.

principles.principle: Know which guidelines bind your game and design within them
principles.why: Age rating, platform, storefront, online service and internal company guidelines must be strictly met or the game can't ship. When they block an intended feature, players may blame the developer without knowing their hands were tied.
principles.how: Gather all applicable guidelines at the start and check planned visuals and features against them before production.
principles.anti_pattern: Discovering a guideline conflict after the feature is built.

principles.principle: Write guidelines with a clear purpose and room for leniency
principles.why: Whether or not a guideline exists, people make the decisions, and sometimes guidelines fit and sometimes they don't. The goal is to end up with something good.
principles.how: When you author rules for a franchise or team, state why each exists and allow justified exceptions.
principles.anti_pattern: Enforcing guidelines rigidly where they clearly don't fit.
principles.example: Tetris allows some exceptions for arcade games where profitability can be an issue.
principles.quote: I think if possible, guidelines should allow for a little leniency.

summary: Treat making games better and coming up with new ideas as learnable topics. That is what this channel exists to teach.
takeaways: The channel teaches how to make games better
It also covers how to come up with new ideas

principles.principle: Study improving games and generating new ideas as learnable skills
principles.why: Sakurai frames how to make games better and how to come up with new ideas as topics that can be taught, and calls teaching them his ultimate goal for the channel.
principles.how: Treat improving an existing design and generating new ideas as two distinct skills to study and practice deliberately.
principles.quote: If you're wondering how to make games better or how to come up with new ideas, I delve into those topics on this very channel.

summary: Late optimization or differences between dev hardware and retail units can silently change the difficulty you tuned, so re-check on the final build and the real production unit, and when a launch problem is too risky to fix at its core, patch it with narrow, contained changes.
takeaways: Optimization changed Meteos' speed because speed tracked processing
Tune and verify on the real production unit
Trust repeated team reports even without a known cause
Patch late problems narrowly to avoid mass re-testing

principles.principle: Re-verify difficulty after optimization when game speed tracks processing speed
principles.why: In Meteos, game speed was directly tied to processing speed, so late optimization sped the game up and made it harder than intended, after tuning was done.
principles.how: Identify any timing tied to processing speed and replay difficulty-critical content on the final optimized build before release.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating smoother performance as purely a win when it also changes game speed.
principles.example: Meteos: some planets' sequences became tough to finish in the time allotted.

principles.principle: Do final tuning checks on the real production unit, not a dev board
principles.why: Sakurai tuned Mushiking on a roughly one-square-meter custom dev board and never played the actual unit. On the production hardware, the Mushi got hungry faster than expected.
principles.how: Before sign-off, play the finished game on retail hardware and compare timing-sensitive values against your dev setup.
principles.anti_pattern: Tuning exclusively on development hardware.
principles.example: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking.

principles.principle: Fix post-launch difficulty problems with contained tweaks, not core rewrites
principles.why: Adjusting the core CPU functions or each mode's difficulty would have meant bug-testing many game elements again, so narrower fixes were the only practical option.
principles.how: Lower the difficulty of specific encounters or add an easier difficulty option through a patch, leaving core systems untouched.
principles.anti_pattern: Rewriting core AI or global difficulty late, forcing wide re-testing.
principles.example: Smash Ultimate: Challenger fights made easier and a Very Easy difficulty added to World of Light.

summary: Make the first frame of every damage reaction an extreme, asymmetric pain pose that looks nothing like standby. Hitstop holds that frame on screen, so a hit should read instantly, even from far away.
takeaways: The first damage frame is held by hitstop; make it extreme
Damage poses must look nothing like standby
Choose reactions by hit height and hit strength
Twist bodies so silhouettes read during knockback
Check stance changes don't push targets out of combos

principles.principle: Make the first damage frame an extreme pain pose unlike standby
principles.why: Hitstop freezes that first frame, so it's what players actually see. An extreme pose that's nothing like standby makes the hit readable even from far away.
principles.how: Author the hitstop frame as an exaggerated pain pose and blend into it briefly from the pose at impact instead of snapping.
principles.anti_pattern: Damage poses that resemble the idle/standby pose.
principles.example: Smash Bros. damage reactions. Kirby's extreme damage pose drawn in the Kirby Super Star design document.
principles.quote: The damage pose and standby pose can be quite similar in some games, but we like to go for something more extreme that's nothing like the standby pose.

principles.principle: Break symmetry and twist bodies so hit reactions read as silhouettes
principles.why: Twisting the body lets the arms and legs read clearly, which wouldn't happen if the character just flew sideways, so both players feel the impact.
principles.how: In every damage and knockback pose, rotate the torso against the hips and separate the limbs from the body outline.
principles.anti_pattern: Stiff, symmetric, side-on knockback poses.
principles.example: Smash Bros. knockback animations.
principles.quote: For all our damage animations, we emphasize breaking a character's symmetry and making their silhouette clearly legible.

principles.principle: Choose damage reactions by impact height and hit strength
principles.why: Picking the reaction closest to the point of impact, scaled by strength, makes each hit look like it landed where and how hard it did.
principles.how: Build high/middle/low reactions selected by the nearest impact point, each in small/medium/large strengths on the ground (nine total), plus a separate knockback set.
principles.anti_pattern: One generic flinch for every hit.
principles.example: Smash Bros.' nine ground damage reaction types.

principles.principle: Check hit-reaction stance changes don't shove targets out of combos
principles.why: Changing a character's stance on hit can move their top node, so a target may slide backward and the rest of a combo misses.
principles.how: Test multi-hit strings against every reaction stance and correct root/top-node offsets so targets stay in place.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting the animation's root motion drift the target away during a combo.
principles.example: Smash Bros.: a neutral attack combo missing because the hit fighter moved back.

summary: Keep an official website as the home base for all your game's information, shaped around your game rather than a standard template, and if people can't see your game's depth, build your own channel (like a players' guide) to explain it.
takeaways: Official sites remain the home base for information
Shape the site to fit your game
When press ignores you, publish your own players' guide
Social media may shift the website's role

principles.principle: Keep an official website as the home base for all game information
principles.why: People dig into websites less now that social media delivers short bursts, but a game still needs one place that delivers all its information.
principles.how: Maintain one canonical site, review its layout and every update yourself, and run it alongside a blog and official social accounts.
principles.anti_pattern: Scattering information only across social posts.
principles.example: Smash Ultimate's site, which Sakurai helps lay out and checks with every update.
principles.quote: In the end, it's still important to have a place to deliver all your information.

principles.principle: Structure your site around your game's content, not a standard template
principles.why: Smash has a huge variety of elements, so its site goes in depth to match, holding far more than the average game site.
principles.how: Build sections from your actual content (characters, modes, techniques, online, stages, music, events) and add features the game needs, like a music player.
principles.anti_pattern: A generic site made "in a standard fashion."
principles.example: Smash Ultimate's site: fighters, 100+ stages, Pokémon and Assist Trophies, music player, fighter reveals, tournaments.
principles.quote: Instead of just making a site in a standard fashion, you want to find a form that best fits your game.

principles.principle: When others misread your game, explain its push and pull yourself
principles.why: A game unlike anything before runs into preconceptions. Magazines ignored Sakurai's documentation, so he built his own channel, and proactively finding new solutions paid off later.
principles.how: Write a clear guide to how your game plays and where its depth lies, and publish it yourself if press won't.
principles.anti_pattern: Waiting for press or partners to discover your game's depth.
principles.example: Smash Bros. DOJO!!, the players' guide site Sakurai hand-coded for the original Smash Bros.
principles.quote: In challenging situations like that, proactively searching for new solutions will ultimately prove fruitful in the future.

summary: While you're writing a proposal, don't talk about it or post about it. Hold the "internal pressure" in, pour it into the document, and consult others only once it's finished.
takeaways: Keep proposals secret until the draft is finished
Talking about ideas releases pressure and weakens them
Consult and brainstorm only after the draft exists
Don't vent ideas or progress on social media
Imagine audience reactions to fuel your work

principles.principle: Keep a proposal to yourself until the first draft is finished
principles.why: Discussing ideas makes you feel fulfilled and releases the internal pressure that gives a proposal its force. A document written without sharing a word burns hotter than a compiled brainstorm.
principles.how: Whenever you want to talk about the idea, write it into the document instead. Consult colleagues for weak points only once the draft is done.
principles.anti_pattern: Talking an idea through before it's written, or substituting a group brainstorm for your own draft.
principles.example: Sakurai's balloon and pressure-cooker metaphors.
principles.quote: In other words, by releasing pressure, the ideas in your mind lose their power.

principles.principle: Don't post ideas or progress on social media while creating
principles.why: Posting ideas or progress vents the same pressure that should go into the work.
principles.how: Hold back social media updates about a project while it's taking shape and put that energy into the work.
principles.anti_pattern: Sharing work-in-progress for the instant satisfaction of reactions.
principles.quote: Posting your ideas or progress on social media will vent your pressure—which you don't want.

principles.principle: Picture how people will react to fuel the work
principles.why: Imagining how your pitch audience and later your players will react, and which parts they'll love, gives you the strength to push on.
principles.how: While writing and developing, picture specific reactions to specific parts of the game and use them as motivation.

summary: When knockback is your core mechanic, give each attack its own set of knockback parameters (direction, a multiplier, a guaranteed minimum with scaling, and an optional fixed value) so every hit can be tuned to land and feel right at any damage level.
takeaways: Knockback grows with attack damage and target's damage
Knockback can go any direction, even following the attacker
Weight and fall speed change the knockback arc
A guaranteed minimum, kept in check by scaling
Fixed knockback keeps multi-hit moves connecting

principles.principle: Make knockback grow with attack damage and the target's accumulated damage
principles.why: In Smash, attacks don't just deplete health. Knockback is at the heart of the game's essence, so it must scale with both the hit and the target's state.
principles.how: Compute launch strength from the attack's damage and the target's damage percentage, then adjust the arc by the target's weight and fall velocity.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating attacks as simple health subtraction in a knockback-centered game.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. attack parameters, unchanged in structure since the original game.
principles.quote: "Knockback" is at the heart of its game essence, so we have to make a few unique considerations.

principles.principle: Use fixed knockback on early hits of multi-hit moves
principles.why: If the later hits failed to land because the opponent's damage was too low or too high, the move would break. Fixed knockback makes the reaction identical at any damage.
principles.how: Give every hit but the last a fixed, damage-independent knockback, and give the finisher standard knockback.
principles.anti_pattern: Damage-scaled knockback on the connecting hits of a multi-hit move.
principles.example: Mario's Super Jump Punch.
principles.quote: It would be quite the problem if later hits didn't land because the opponent's damage was too low or too high.

principles.principle: Guarantee a minimum knockback, kept in check by scaling
principles.why: A launcher should cause at least some reaction on a barely damaged opponent, but simply adding a minimum would make knockback too big.
principles.how: Add a per-attack minimum knockback value and pair it with knockback scaling, plus a multiplier for fine-tuning.
principles.anti_pattern: Adding a flat minimum with no scaling, which inflates every launch.
principles.example: Smash Bros. upward launch attacks against low-damage opponents.

principles.principle: Let knockback direction follow the attacker's travel to sustain aerial combos
principles.why: Smash allows knockback in any direction, and a modifier that reacts to the attacker's movement helps more hits of an aerial combo land.
principles.how: Give each attack a free launch angle plus an optional flag that biases the launch toward the attacker's direction of travel.
principles.anti_pattern: Locking knockback to a few fixed directions when combos need to follow the target.
principles.example: Smash Bros. aerial combos.

summary: When you arrange beloved game music, the original as players heard it in the game is the authority, including its quirks, its structure and even changes forced by the hardware, over what music theory says.
takeaways: The original as heard in-game beats music theory
Reproduce the original's quirks faithfully
Mirror hardware-driven structure, like vocals ending after verse one
Keep language versions distinct, down to intonation
Clarify terms when feedback seems ignored

principles.principle: Treat the original as heard in-game as the authority when arranging
principles.why: Players' memories come from playing the original, so an arrangement must not detract from their past experience, however unconventional the original is.
principles.how: Identify the main melody and key features by what players heard in the game (and its ports), and reproduce quirks like an on-beat/off-beat shift faithfully.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting music theory overrule what the original actually sounded like.
principles.example: Athena: Sakurai heard melody A as the main melody, while musically it was B. Its on-beat/off-beat shift was reproduced in Smash.
principles.quote: However you cut it, when arranging beloved songs, the original piece is always right.

principles.principle: Mirror the original's hardware-driven structure in arrangements
principles.why: In the original Psycho Soldier, the music switched to the internal audio processor after the first verse, and that shape is part of what players remember.
principles.how: Where the original lost vocals or changed character because of the hardware, use an instrumental section there, and keep separate language versions with their own verse counts and intonation.
principles.anti_pattern: Normalizing a song's structure to modern conventions.
principles.example: Psycho Soldier in Smash Ultimate: Japanese recreates three verses. English plays verse one, an instrumental, then verse one again.

principles.principle: When revisions contradict your feedback, check that your terms match
principles.why: Arrangement changes on Athena kept coming back as the opposite of Sakurai's feedback because he and the musicians meant different things by "main melody."
principles.how: When notes seem ignored, play the reference together and agree on what each term refers to before giving more feedback.
principles.anti_pattern: Repeating the same notes louder without checking definitions.
principles.example: Athena arrangement for Smash Bros.

summary: Size menu items by importance, with the most-used modes as the biggest icons, so players reach what matters fastest, and watch for the costs to versatility and translation.
takeaways: Bigger icons for more-used modes
Size signals priority and eases access
Weighted layouts suit games with unequal button importance
Icon labels struggle with wider languages

principles.principle: Size menu items by how often players use them
principles.why: Size shows which modes take priority, so players reach the most-used options fastest. It's all about ease of access.
principles.how: Rank menu options by expected use and make the top ones the largest tiles or icons, shrinking rarely used ones.
principles.anti_pattern: Presenting every option as an equal-weight list when some matter far more.
principles.example: Menus from Meteos onward, including the Smash Bros. menu.
principles.quote: The size indicates which modes take priority and what's important.

principles.principle: Weight buttons unequally only when the game's actions are unequal
principles.why: The GameCube's big A and small X/Y let you feel which button to press, but in games where all buttons have equal value that layout is harder to use and costs versatility.
principles.how: Make the dominant action's input the most prominent, and keep inputs equal when the game uses them equally (e.g., face-button menu navigation).
principles.anti_pattern: Unequal button emphasis in a game where every button matters equally.
principles.example: The GameCube controller.

principles.principle: Test icon menu layouts against wider languages early
principles.why: Icon menus are hard to fit in languages that take more horizontal space. The Smash layout worked best in Japanese.
principles.how: Mock up icon labels in your longest target language before locking the layout.
principles.anti_pattern: Designing labels for one language and leaving translation to squeeze in later.
principles.example: Smash Bros. menu translations.

summary: Pick your target audience first, then set how much risk your rules carry. More risk means more thrill but less broad appeal, so a beginner-focused game should deliberately hold back.
takeaways: Too much game essence reduces broad appeal
Risk and reward scale in near-perfect proportion
Low-risk beginner games trade thrill for accessibility
Be kind to beginners; difficulty perception varies
Choose your target audience from your concept

principles.principle: Choose your target audience first, then set risk to match
principles.why: Who you target should depend on your game's design and concept. A minor risk to an experienced player can be a brick wall to a beginner.
principles.how: Write down the target player, then tune risk dials (threat range, hit count, escape tools, control inertia) to their skill.
principles.anti_pattern: Tuning risk to your own skill level and assuming everyone perceives difficulty the same way.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land was built for beginners and accomplishes exactly what it set out to do.
principles.quote: Start by understanding how game essence arises, and use that knowledge to hone in on a target audience.

principles.principle: Scale reward with risk; accept that low risk means low thrill
principles.why: Balanced correctly, risk and reward scale in almost perfect proportion: a more intense risk gives more intense joy, and low risk brings low reward.
principles.how: When you lower risk for accessibility, expect less intense satisfaction and judge the design by whether it serves its audience.
principles.anti_pattern: Expecting a low-risk game to be as thrilling as a high-risk one.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land is less thrilling than Super Mario Bros., where you turn extreme risk next to enemies into a counterattack.
principles.quote: Risk and reward, when balanced correctly, should scale in almost perfect proportion.

principles.principle: Hold back rules that boost push and pull but hurt clarity
principles.why: You can always add rules to increase game essence, but overcomplicated rulesets make the experience hard to grasp and reduce broad appeal.
principles.how: Before adding a rule to deepen push and pull, check whether your target players could still grasp the game, and skip it if not.
principles.anti_pattern: Piling on mechanics for depth until the game is hard to understand.
principles.quote: Sometimes, it's important to hold back from a chance to boost game essence.

principles.principle: Give beginners tools that neutralize threats before risk gets high
principles.why: In Kirby's Dream Land, inhale stops enemies while the risk is still low, six hits of health and on-demand flight soften penalties, and that's what makes it approachable.
principles.how: For a beginner audience, add generous neutralizing range, a forgiving health pool and an escape option from the steepest penalties.
principles.anti_pattern: Harsh penalties like one-hit deaths or heavy inertia in a game meant for newcomers.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land: inhale, a spit attack with more range than the inhale, six hits of health, flight to avoid pits.
principles.quote: We should be kind to beginners.

summary: A tour of one-of-a-kind items from Sakurai's career. It is mostly anecdotes, but it includes a reminder that he first got through Sega's doors by submitting a game proposal to a public promotion before he worked in the industry.
takeaways: Rare gifts and autographs from Sakurai's career
A late-1980s Sega proposal contest got him inside Sega
Sega preserves an After Burner cabinet with 3D-printed parts

principles.principle: Submit game proposals to open calls even before entering the industry
principles.why: Sakurai's late-1980s entry to a Sega proposal promotion won him Associate Planner Certificate No. 004 and a visit to Sega before he had entered the industry.
principles.how: Enter publisher or studio proposal contests and open calls with a concrete mechanic idea.
principles.example: Sega Associate Planner Certificate No. 004, for a proposal like an action-focused Active Time Battle system.
principles.quote: In the late 1980s, Sega had a promotion where people could submit game proposals— which is where I won this.

principles.principle: When filming solo without zoom, cut to close-up photos and video
principles.why: Sakurai shot the video alone and couldn't zoom while talking, so he cut to close-ups to show the details.
principles.how: Shoot close-up photos or clips of small details in advance and edit them in.
principles.quote: I can't zoom in while I'm talking, so I'll cut to close-up photos and videos instead.

summary: Don't let your animation tool's interpolation water down the key poses. Reach the key frames fast, spend the time on the anticipation and the strike, and push the poses further than the source, so 3D moves stay as snappy as their 2D originals.
takeaways: Interpolation can make same-timed animations feel slow
Reach key frames quickly; skimp on in-betweens
Hold anticipation, then snap through key poses
Exaggerate poses beyond the original
Follow-through shouldn't reverse the attack or match standby

principles.principle: Reach key poses fast and minimize interpolated in-between frames
principles.why: Tools interpolate conveniently, but interpolated frames overpower the key poses and make an animation feel slow even when its frame count matches the original.
principles.how: Scrub interpolated attacks and cut in-between time so key frames arrive quickly, judging snappiness by eye rather than frame count.
principles.anti_pattern: Accepting default interpolation between reference poses.
principles.example: An 8-frame kick in Smash Ultimate that felt slow when interpolated and much snappier in the release version, at the same 8 frames.
principles.quote: But convenience doesn't mean quality.

principles.principle: Hold the anticipation, then snap through key poses
principles.why: Saving time for the lead-in and attack keeps momentum. Key poses shown for even one frame each still leave an impression when the attack hits.
principles.how: Pull the wind-up further back, hold it relatively long, then pass through each key pose in as little as one frame.
principles.anti_pattern: Spreading time evenly across the motion.
principles.example: Ryu's crouching heavy punch in Smash Ultimate: forearm pulled back, long-held anticipation, three original key poses on screen one frame each.
principles.quote: Make sure your animations really come out swinging!

principles.principle: Exaggerate key poses beyond the source material
principles.why: Moving from 2D to 3D loses momentum, so poses need more energy than the original key frames to feel as strong.
principles.how: When adapting reference art, push each key pose further, e.g., a deeper wind-up or a different first frame for more momentum.
principles.anti_pattern: Copying the source poses exactly and expecting the same punch.
principles.example: Ryu's first frame differs in Smash to express more momentum than his crouching start.
principles.quote: If possible, try to give the poses even more energy than the original key frames.

principles.principle: Give follow-through its own path, distinct from the standby pose
principles.why: The original's backwards playback doesn't translate to 3D, and a follow-through that matches standby loses the motion's character.
principles.how: Animate a separate return trajectory after the strike, kept close to the original's feel, that doesn't simply end at idle.
principles.anti_pattern: Reversing the attack animation or ending on the standby pose.
principles.example: Ryu's uppercut follow-through in Smash Ultimate.
principles.quote: You don't want your follow-through to be the same as your standby pose.

summary: Design your rewards in the planning stage and pick types that fit your concept. If making the character stronger would undermine the game (as in a fighting game), reward with unlocks, collectibles and goals instead.
takeaways: Plan rewards in the planning stage
Character growth is the most effective reward, if it fits
In fighting games, growth makes the 'real' game start late
Cheap formats like stickers scale better than trophies
Objectives themselves are rewards; motivation and reward intertwine
games: Super Smash Bros. for 3DS / Wii U

principles.principle: Design reward systems during the planning stage
principles.why: You must reward players, but that's impossible if you have nothing to give them. A game without rewards or new developments is drab.
principles.how: In the planning doc, list every reward type and when it arrives, and add systems if the list is thin.
principles.anti_pattern: Bolting rewards on late in development.
principles.quote: Hence, we should be thinking about compensation right from a game's planning and design stages.

principles.principle: Match reward type to concept; avoid stat growth in fighting games
principles.why: Getting stronger is the most effective reward, but in a fighting game where characters grow stronger, the "real" game seems to start only at max level.
principles.how: If growth would undermine competition, reward with unlocks (e.g., fighters earned by beating incoming challengers), collectibles and options instead.
principles.anti_pattern: Character-strengthening progression in a game whose fun depends on a fixed baseline.
principles.example: Smash Bros.: fighter unlocks via challengers, coins with no stronger gear to buy.

principles.principle: Choose collectible formats by production cost so content can scale
principles.why: Trophies needed models and descriptions and inflated production costs. Stickers and spirits needed neither, so far more characters could be included.
principles.how: Prefer lightweight formats (images plus a gameplay effect) when you want large collections.
principles.anti_pattern: Making every collectible a fully modeled, written item when volume matters.
principles.example: Smash trophies (Melee to 3DS/Wii U) vs. stickers (Brawl) and spirits.

principles.principle: Use a goal grid that reveals neighboring objectives as each clears
principles.why: Objectives are rewards in their own right. The grid gives players things to work toward, more than the rewards themselves.
principles.how: Lay out conditions as panels; clearing one breaks it and shows the unlock conditions of adjacent panels.
principles.anti_pattern: Going overboard with reward systems.
principles.example: Kirby Air Ride's Checklist, later Smash's Challenges, predating console achievement systems.
principles.quote: You could say that game objectives are rewards in their own right, and that motivation and reward are simply two sides of the same coin.

summary: Graphics and game essence feed each other: gameplay gives environments their "presence," and visuals decide whether players try the game at all. So develop the two together and raise both as far as you can.
takeaways: Game essence brings graphics to life
Cautious, deadly gameplay gives environments presence
Storefront banners decide whether players look
Graphics multiply fun; elevate both

principles.principle: Let gameplay give environments presence; match art to how players look
principles.why: Environments are just polygons until gameplay gives them meaning. Frequent deaths make players scrutinize every nook, while the same art at high speed leaves a very different impression.
principles.how: Decide how closely your gameplay makes players inspect the world and put environmental detail where they'll actually look.
principles.anti_pattern: Making environment art without considering the game's pace and threat level.
principles.example: Dark Souls and Sekiro vs. a game with Sonic running at high speed.
principles.quote: The game world is a mirage you can pass straight through.

principles.principle: Make visuals strong enough to draw players in on crowded storefronts
principles.why: On stores like Steam, people use a game's banner to decide whether to look at it. If the visuals don't draw them in, they won't play.
principles.how: Treat banner and key art as critical assets and test whether they make people want to click.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming good gameplay will be found regardless of presentation.
principles.example: Steam's almost endless lineup.
principles.quote: If your visuals don't draw players in, people won't play your game.

principles.principle: Elevate graphics and game essence together rather than trading one off
principles.why: Graphics multiply a game's fun, and essence and visuals affect each other, so it's best to strike a balance and raise both.
principles.how: Develop art alongside mechanics and review them together so each reinforces the other.
principles.anti_pattern: Dismissing graphics as unrelated to fun.
principles.quote: In that sense, you could say that graphics multiply the fun of a game.

summary: Use billboards (flat images that always face the camera) for particles, light flashes and cheap objects because they render cheaply, but know their weaknesses: they look odd when the camera circles them, and misused Y-axis billboards look too skinny.
takeaways: Billboards are camera-facing two-polygon images
Particles and flashes are mostly billboards
Low render cost suits intangible effects
Billboards look odd when the camera rotates around them
Misused Y-axis billboards look too skinny

principles.principle: Build particles and light flashes from billboards to save render cost
principles.why: 2D objects have a relatively low rendering cost, and billboards suit intangible effects such as flashes of light.
principles.how: Compose explosions and flashes from camera-facing billboard particles, then layer extras like sparks on top.
principles.example: Smash Bros. explosions, which are flat images when paused and viewed from another angle.
principles.quote: 2D objects have a relatively low rendering cost. And billboards are just perfect for intangible effects such as flashes of light.

principles.principle: Mix billboards with 3D parts to make simple objects cheaply
principles.why: A single image can stand in for a whole object, and a billboard body can carry 3D-modeled details.
principles.how: Billboard simple round or distant objects, and attach modeled parts where depth matters.
principles.anti_pattern: Using billboards for objects that the camera circles closely.
principles.example: Super Mario 64's rolling iron balls, and King Bob-omb's billboard body with 3D eyes and crown.

principles.principle: Check billboards under camera rotation; use Y-axis billboards carefully
principles.why: Billboards look strange when the camera rotates around them, and Y-axis billboards misused for effects feel too skinny.
principles.how: Orbit the camera around every billboarded asset in review and switch to a model where it breaks.
principles.anti_pattern: Misusing Y-axis billboards for effects.
principles.example: Smash Bros. food items, traditionally billboards.

summary: When new hardware offers a new input, find a control that uses what only it can do (like reading how fast the analog stick reaches its edge to trigger a dash), but don't shoehorn in every possible use.
takeaways: Flick input reads how fast the stick hits its edge
One gesture replaces double-taps or button-plus-direction dashes
Tilt-based walking speed makes controls feel physical
Offer sensitivity settings to curb accidental dashes
Explore new peripherals, but don't shoehorn functions in

principles.principle: Trigger dashes with a fast flick of the stick to its edge
principles.why: Older dashes took two steps (double-tap) or two buttons (B-button dash). Reading how fast the stick reaches its edge gives one simple, physical action.
principles.how: Scale walk speed by tilt, and start a dash when the stick travels from neutral to its edge within a short time.
principles.anti_pattern: Requiring a double-tap or a held button for a basic movement action.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. (N64), where flick input was localized as "Tap."
principles.quote: Adjusting walking speed based on how much you tilt the analog stick lets you not only feel the controls, but also understand them more easily.

principles.principle: Make flick sensitivity adjustable to reduce accidental dashes
principles.why: Flick input's downside is dashing by accident, and players differ in how hard they push the stick.
principles.how: Expose the flick threshold as a player setting.
principles.anti_pattern: A fixed threshold that causes unwanted dashes.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's flick sensitivity option.

principles.principle: Explore a new peripheral's unique abilities, but don't shoehorn them in
principles.why: New hardware can enable distinctive controls, as the analog stick did for Smash, but forcing every possible function in doesn't help the game.
principles.how: List what the new input can do that older inputs can't and adopt only the uses that fit your design, e.g., one flick gesture for dash and dodge.
principles.anti_pattern: Using every feature of a peripheral just because it's there.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's flick dash and dodge. Brawl deliberately not using every Nunchuk or pointer function.
principles.quote: When designing games for hardware that features new peripherals, you should think for a moment about what's possible with those peripherals.

summary: Play the foundational arcade games of 1978–1987 yourself. Many building blocks of modern games started there, and their scoring rules show how to tempt players into taking risks.
takeaways: You can't discuss game history without arcade games
1978–1987 arcades evolved dramatically in ten years
Greed-based scoring tempts players into risk
Asymmetric fail rules make mismatched play fun
Each clever idea built on the last

principles.principle: Reward greed with bigger scores for chaining riskier plays
principles.why: Several classic arcade games make the high-scoring play the dangerous one, so players are constantly tempted to push their luck.
principles.how: Pay escalating points for chaining risky actions, such as eating several fleeing enemies in one power-up, clearing escorts before the leader, or crushing enemies with a dropped object.
principles.anti_pattern: Making the safe play also the highest-scoring play.
principles.example: Galaxian flagships worth more after escorts. Escalating points for fleeing blue ghosts. Crushing with rocks instead of inflating.
principles.quote: It's really tempting to get greedy. After all, you get more points the more fleeing blue ghosts you can eat in one go.

principles.principle: Let danger rise as a result of the player's own progress
principles.why: In Space Invaders, the fewer invaders remain, the faster they move, so careless clearing lets them reach you quickly. Strategy emerges from that rule.
principles.how: Tie enemy speed or aggression to how many threats remain, so the order of clearing becomes a strategic choice.
principles.example: Space Invaders: clear one column at a time from the ends.
principles.quote: Once you have fewer invaders to deal with, they'll move faster left and right

principles.principle: Use asymmetric fail conditions so mismatched players enjoy the same game
principles.why: Sakurai gave himself a one-hit loss while the guest played to game over, and framed it as shared fun rather than a contest with a winner and a loser.
principles.how: In co-play between players of very different skill, give the stronger player a stricter fail condition and move on together when either fails.
principles.anti_pattern: Framing every mismatched session as a strict head-to-head competition.
principles.example: The Space Invaders Decade challenge with Arino Kacho.
principles.quote: But I don't think we have to frame this as a competition with one winner and one loser.

principles.principle: Study your genre's foundational games firsthand
principles.why: You can't talk about gaming history without arcade games. Playing them shows how clever ideas like horizontal scrolling, separate bomb buttons, fuel gauges, jumping and parallax built on each other.
principles.how: Play the early titles in your genre and note which mechanic each introduced.
principles.example: Scramble's groundwork for side-scrollers like Gradius. Donkey Kong's jumping. Moon Patrol's parallax scrolling.
principles.quote: But you just can't talk about gaming history without including arcade games in the mix, I'd say.
